dek: Bridal Wreath Falls is the one waterfall we cover in Saguaro National Park, on the Tucson side near Tanque Verde. Here are the trail name, fees and when to go.
overview: Saguaro National Park is the cactus forest on both sides of Tucson, Arizona, with a district on the east and another on the west. The one waterfall we cover inside the park is Bridal Wreath Falls, which our directory files under Tanque Verde on the eastern side, in Pima County.
This is a desert park, and we don't have a published record of when Bridal Wreath Falls flows. Ask a ranger or check recent trail reports before you plan a trip around the water.
fallsIntro: Bridal Wreath Falls is the only waterfall in Saguaro National Park with a page in our directory. Our map file names the Bridal Wreath Falls Trail but doesn't list a distance, so confirm the mileage with the park before you set out.
flow: The nearest stream gauge with a complete record is on Rincon Creek near Tucson (USGS 09485000), about 7 miles from the falls. Between 2019 and 2024 its average daily flow peaked in February at about 17 cubic feet per second and dropped to zero in May.
That is a desert creek, not the waterfall itself, so use it as a rough picture of when water moves through the area rather than a flow report for Bridal Wreath Falls.
feesLead: Entry is a modest per-vehicle fee, sold as a dated receipt for one private, non-commercial vehicle. The park's fee page doesn't mention timed entry.
access: Saguaro sits on both the east and west sides of Tucson, and the two districts are a separate drive apart. We file Bridal Wreath Falls under Tanque Verde, on the east side, about 5 miles away in a straight line. Use the trail name and the coordinates on the waterfall page to find the trailhead, and confirm the route with the park.
safety: Heat shapes a visit here. The park's weather page says ranger programs are limited in late spring and summer because of the heat, and that more programs run in winter. That is about being outside in the desert, not about how much water is in the falls. We have no waterfall-specific warning on file, so carry plenty of water and ask at a visitor center about current trail conditions.
